questions.q: What is Charley's age and occupation as stated in the story?
questions.a: Charley is 31 years old and works in an office (he mentions working late at the office). A wrong answer (e.g., saying he is a student or retired) reveals the student has not read the basic factual details of the protagonist, which are essential for grounding any character analysis.

questions.q: The psychiatrist calls Charley's experience a "waking-dream wish fulfillment." Explain in your own words what this means and why Charley's wife gets mad.
questions.a: The psychiatrist means Charley's discovery of the third level is a psychological escape mechanism — a fantasy created by his subconscious to flee the stresses of modern life (insecurity, fear, war, worry). Charley's wife gets mad because the psychiatrist said Charley is "unhappy," which she interprets as a criticism of their marriage or her role. A wrong answer that takes the psychiatrist's words literally (e.g., "Charley was asleep") shows the student misses the psychological interpretation and the marital dynamic.

questions.q: Charley says, "I wasn't trying to escape from anything; I just wanted to get home to Louisa." Apply the concept of dramatic irony: why is this statement ironic given what happens later?
questions.a: The statement is ironic because Charley unconsciously does exactly what he denies: he escapes into the third level (1894) to avoid modern anxieties. His conscious intention (getting home) is overridden by his subconscious desire for escape, which the story reveals through the third level's existence. A wrong answer that says "it's not ironic because he really just wanted to go home" shows the student cannot distinguish between character's stated motive and authorial implication.

questions.q: Analyze Charley's stamp collecting. How does it function as both a character trait and a thematic symbol? Use two pieces of textual evidence.
questions.a: Charley's stamp collecting is a "temporary refuge from reality" (psychiatrist's words) and a link to his grandfather's peaceful era. Evidence: (1) The psychiatrist calls it a refuge; (2) Charley defends it by noting his grandfather started the collection when times were "nice and peaceful." This shows Charley's nostalgia and desire for a simpler past, which foreshadows his third-level journey. A wrong answer that only says "he likes stamps" misses the symbolic and psychological layers.

questions.q: Evaluate Charley's reliability as a narrator. Is the third level "real" in the story's world? Defend your interpretation with evidence from the ending.
questions.a: Charley is an unreliable narrator because his perception is colored by his desire to escape. The third level's reality is ambiguous: the story presents it as a psychological phenomenon (psychiatrist's diagnosis), but the ending with Sam's letter and the first-day cover dated 1894 suggests a fantastical possibility. A strong evaluation acknowledges both readings: as a metaphor for escapism, it's "unreal"; as a fantasy narrative, it's "real." A wrong answer that insists on only one reading (e.g., "it's all a dream" or "it's definitely real") shows inability to handle textual ambiguity.

questions.q: Create a diary entry from Charley's perspective on the night he discovers the third level, revealing his inner conflict between his rational self and his escapist longing. Use at least two phrases from the text.
questions.a: A good diary entry will show Charley's rational side ("I'm just an ordinary guy") and his longing ("I wanted two tickets for that... peaceful world"). It might include phrases like "waking-dream wish fulfillment" and "Galesburg, Illinois." A poor entry will only recount plot events without internal conflict, indicating the student hasn't grasped Charley's psychological duality.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Character analysis of the ______ involves examining the main character's personality traits, motivations, conflicts, development, and role in advancing the story's themes, using textual evidence such as actions, dialogue, thoughts, and narrator's description.
Fill in the blank: Start by asking the student: "Have you ever felt so ______ by modern life that you wished you could just step into a simpler past?
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can write a structured character sketch of Charley that identifies at least three distinct personality traits, supports each with specific textual evidence, explains how Charley's psychological state drives the plot, and connects his characterization to the story's central theme of escapism.
